text#20.88
the Pakistan Nursing Council from where he was fired at the instance of the complainant due to which he planned his revenge with his brother Raqeeb and cousin Hayat, both petitioners in this case, who are Elite Force commandos in KPK; that the CDRs demonstrated that the accused switched off their phones on the date of occurrence when they reached near Tarnol coming from KPK, and that this was established through geo-fencing, and that the phones of all the accused were switched back on, on or about the same time when they returned to Charsadda. The investigation officer further elaborated that the safe city cameras recorded their car’s entry in Islamabad, which corresponded with the time of switching-off of their mobile phones per the CDRs, and that the said car was recovered from the accused. Learned counsel also added that the pre-arrest bail applications were dismissed for non-prosecution (this is confirmed by the bail order of the court below), and that the complainant was never present in the precincts of the trial court on that date. He added further that the complainant wanted proper treatment of his broken arm and, not finding the response satisfactory at PIMS, left for a private hospital about 15 minutes after he was received in the emergency department of PIMS. Above all, he added that the mobile phones as well as the educational certificates reported stolen in the dacoity stand recovered from the accused.
footer#30.88
5
text#40.88
This is a case where the investigation on tentative assessment
text#50.88
inspires prima facie confidence in the prosecution’s case. The geo-fencing results, the phones of all the accused being switched-off at the same time at Tarnol and remaining switched-off for the period that the dacoity was committed and being switched back on in Charsada around the same time the next day, cumulatively support the prosecution’s case. The recoveries of the stolen items, the positive identification parades, and the footage of the car recovered from the accused recorded in the safe city cameras entering Islamabad before the time of occurrence, all tend to connect the dots, which, on a tentative assessment, demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that the accused persons are guilty of the offences they are charged with, all of which except one are non-bailable and carry sentences falling within the ambit of the prohibitory clause of section 497 CrPC.

In order to determine the entitlement or otherwise of the

list#70.88
517. Order for disposal of property regarding which offence committed. (1) When an inquiry or a trial in any Criminal Court is concluded, the Court may make such order as it thinks fit for the disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or otherwise of any property or document produced before it or in its custody or regarding which any offence appears to have been committed or which has been used for the commission of any offence.
text#80.88
(2) When a High Court or Court of Sessions makes such order and cannot through its own officers conveniently deliver the property to the person entitled thereto, such Court may direct that the order be carried effect by the [District Officer (Revenue)].
text#90.88
(3) When an order is made under this section such order shall not, except where the property is livestock or subject to speedy and natural decay, and save as provided by subsection (4), be carried out for one month, or, when an appeal is presented, until such appeal has been disposed of.
text#100.88
(4) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to prohibit any Court from delivering any property under the provisions of sub-section (1) to any person claiming to be entitled to the possession thereof, on his executing a bond with or without sureties to the satisfaction of the Court; engaging to restore such property to the Court if the order made under this section is modified or set aside on appeal.
text#110.88
Above section clearly mentions that when an inquiry or trial is concluded, Court concerned may pass order for the disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or otherwise of any property or document. Sattar appellants were booked in case FIR No. 33 registered at Police Station Anti-Narcotics Force, Peshawar on 31.05.2009 in respect of an offence under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. The allegation leveled by the prosecution was that a trailer-truck being driven by Hussain Shah appellant was intercepted by a raiding party and from a secret cavity of that vehicle Charas weighing 12000 kilograms contained in 600 bags, each bag containing 20 packets, was recovered and samples of the recovered substance had subsequently been tested positive by the

text#20.88

It was maintained by the prosecution that Abdul Sattar appellant was a cleaner and a helper of the driver of that vehicle. After a regular trial the appellants were convicted by the trial court for an offence under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997 and were sentenced to imprisonment for life each and to pay fine which convictions and sentences of the appellants were subsequently upheld and maintained by the High Court. Hence, the present appeal by leave of this Court granted on 27.09.2017.
text#30.88

Leave to appeal had been granted in this case in order to
text#50.88
reappraise the evidence and with the assistance of the learned counsel for the parties we have undertaken that exercise.
text#60.88
3.
text#70.88
Hussain Shah appellant was driving the relevant vehicle
text#80.88
when it was intercepted and from a secret cavity of that vehicle a huge quantity of narcotic substance had been recovered and subsequently a report received from the Chemical Examiner had declared that the recovered substance was Charas. The prosecution witnesses deposing about the alleged recovery were public servants who had no ostensible reason to falsely implicate the said appellant in a case of this nature. The said witnesses had made consistent statements fully incriminating the appellant in the alleged offence. Nothing has been brought to our notice which could possibly be used to doubt the veracity of the said witnesses. Both the courts below had undertaken an exhaustive analysis of the evidence available on the record and had then concurred in their conclusion regarding guilt of the said appellant having been proved beyond reasonable doubt and upon our own independent evaluation of the evidence we have not been able to take a view of the matter different from that concurrently taken by the courts below vis-à-vis the said appellant.

text#30.88
It has been argued before us that the report submitted by
text#40.88
the Chemical Examiner did not mention the necessary protocols followed or tests applied but we have seen the said report available on the record of the trial court and have found that the said report not only referred to the protocols adopted but also to the tests applied and, thus, we have not been able to find any deficiency in the said report. It has further been argued before us that the Chemical Examiner who had prepared the relevant report was not qualified to hold that position and in that connection Rule 3 of the Control of Narcotic Substances (Government Analysts) Rules, 2001 has been relied upon but we have found that there is nothing available on the record to conclude or hold that the Chemical Examiner preparing the relevant report was not qualified to hold that office. Apart from that a Notification is available on the record according to which the relevant Chemical Examiner had been duly notified by the Government as a Federal Government Analyst. The record further shows that the said Chemical Examiner had prepared the relevant report at a time when he was being assisted in the matter by Mrs. Farhana Shaukat who held the degree of M.Sc. Biochemistry and she too was notified by the Government as the Federal Government Analyst through the same Notification. In this view of the matter the objection raised before us regarding the Chemical Examiner in this case not being qualified to hold that office has failed to impress us. Yet another argument was raised before us regarding the trial court having no jurisdiction to take fresh samples from the recovered substance so that they may be examined by the Chemical Examiner but even that argument has not been found by us to be holding much water. The record of the case shows that initially 600 samples taken from the 600 bags recovered from the relevant vehicle had been sent to the Chemical Examiner for analysis but the Chemical Examiner had returned those samples and had required that a sample had to be taken from each and every packet of the substance recovered in this case and such packets were 12000 in number and it was in that backdrop that the trial court had instructed a Magistrate and under the supervision of that Magistrate fresh and separate

Aqeel Ahmed Abbasi J.- The instant petition for leave to appeal is filed by the petitioner under Article 185(3) of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973. The petitioner has challenged the impugned order dated 12.02.2025 passed by the Division Bench of Peshawar High Court, Peshawar in Custom Reference Application No. 154-P/2024, whereby the reference filed under Section 196 of the Customs Act 1969, (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) against the judgment dated 04.11.2024 passed by the Custom Appellate Tribunal, Peshawar (Special Division Bench), was dismissed.

ORDER
text#80.88
Jawwad S. Khawaja, J. These two constitutional petitions (C.P 33 of 2005 and C.P 34
text#90.88
of 2005) have been filed by Engr. Iqbal Zafar Jhagra and Senator Rukhsana Zuberi. The
text#100.88
petitioners have raised a number of issues about the pricing of petrol and natural gas which
text#110.88
have a direct bearing with the enforcement of the fundamental rights of the people of
text#120.88
Pakistan who have to bear the brunt of such prices.
text#130.88
2.
text#140.88
Amongst other things, the petitioners allege that the price at which Compressed
text#150.88
Natural Gas (CNG) is being sold to vehicle owners is not being determined in accordance
text#160.88
with the law and is therefore inflated. There is no denying the fact that CNG prices have
text#170.88
indeed increased over the last few years. According to figures provided by the Secretary,
text#180.88
Ministry of Petroleum, in August 2008, CNG was being sold in Pakistan at the rate of Rs. 33
text#190.88
per kg. Only four years later, in September 2012, it was being sold at Rs. 95 per kg – almost
text#200.88
three time the original prices. The number of citizens affected by this increase is also very
text#210.88
large. According to figures provided by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA), no
text#220.88
less than 3395 licenses for CNG marketing have been granted. The number of users of CNG
text#230.88
whether direct, or as poor commuters traveling on the roofs of buses, who depend on public
text#240.88
transport is estimated to run into millions, and around 12% of the total gas in the national
text#250.88
transmission system is devoted to the CNG sector.
text#260.88
3.
text#270.88
While the petitioners have raised a number of issues, in the present order, we
text#280.88
confine ourselves to only one: the pricing process for CNG. The Court did hear some
text#290.88
arguments about the issue of pricing process of natural gas sold directly to consumers by
text#300.88
SSGC and SNGPL and the impact of unaccounted for natural gas (UFG) losses on its
text#310.88
determination. However, Mr. Abid Hasan Minto, Sr. ASC, learned counsel for SSGC and
text#320.88
SNGPL apprised the Court that the same issue was moot in writs filed before the High
text#330.88
Courts of Sindh and Lahore. In the latter court, arguments have been concluded and the

text#20.88
judgment is presently reserved. Mr. Minto therefore, requested that consideration of the
text#30.88
issue relating to UFG losses be postponed to a date till at least one of the High Courts has
text#40.88
pronounced its judgment. This suggestion has been made to enable all concerned to
text#50.88
examine the reasoning which prevailed with the High Court. The suggestion being
text#60.88
reasonable, we confine ourselves to the issue of CNG pricing, leaving the rest of issues for
text#70.88
subsequent hearings.
text#80.88
4.
text#90.88
It is clear from a review of the relevant laws that the primary responsibility for
text#100.88
determining the sale price of CNG for consumers falls on OGRA. Rule 13 of the Compressed
text#110.88
Natural Gas (Production and Marketing Rules), 1992 states that: “The Authority [OGRA] shall
text#120.88
determine and notify the sale price in accordance with the policy guidelines issued by the Federal
text#130.88
Government, from time to time. (2) No license[e] shall charge price from its consumer which is higher
text#140.88
than the sale price notified by the Authority, [OGRA] from time to time.”
text#150.88
5.
text#160.88
It is correct, therefore, that the policy guidelines issued by the Federal Government
text#170.88
are to be given consideration by OGRA. Section 21 of the OGRA Ordinance also states in
text#180.88
similar vein that “… the Authority [OGRA] shall comply with the policy guidelines [issued by the
text#190.88
Federal Government]…” If read out of context, these provisions could create the impression
text#200.88
that in matters such as price determination, the Federal Government enjoys co-extensive
text#210.88
powers with OGRA; or that, at least, its policy guidelines trump any other considerations
text#220.88
which OGRA may have before it. However, this reading of the text runs against the overall
text#230.88
scheme and text of the OGRA Ordinance. Policy guidelines are exactly what they purport to
text#240.88
be i.e. guidelines at most. The statute envisages that the regulatory functions are to be
text#250.88
performed by an Authority which is “independent in the performance of its functions”, (S. 3(2)).
text#260.88
This independence is actualized by laying down stringent objective appointment criteria of
text#270.88
“eminent professionals of known integrity and competence” for key decision-makers (Section 3),
text#280.88
vesting them with security of tenure (S. 3(8) and S. 5) and funding OGRA through its own
text#290.88
statutory fund (S. 18). Clearly, all of these measures were taken by the legislature to provide
text#300.88
OGRA with a strong measure of independence from the Federal Government. The measures
text#310.88
would be rendered entirely superfluous if we construe Section 21 of the Ordinance and Rule
text#320.88
14 in a manner which makes OGRA bound by the directives of the Federal Government.
text#330.88
Since, the general principle of statutory interpretation is that the language of the legislature
text#340.88
must not be rendered superfluous, we take it that that Section 21 and Rule 14 imply only

text#120.89
The petitioners, in the instant petition,
text#130.87
have made the following prayers:-
text#140.88
"Wherefore, it is respectfully prayed that the classification, allocation and assignment and consequent licensing of the 850MHz block by the respondent No.1 and No.2 and approvals granted thereof by the respondent No.3 be declared without authority and jurisdiction and hence illegal and void; It is further prayed that the respondent No.1 may be directed to strictly act in accordance with law and promulgate the necessary regulations mandated under section 42 of the PTRA 1996 prior to taking any further actions; It is further prayed that the respondent No.3 may be directed to properly and lawfully establish the Board of the Respondent No.1 by virtue of appointment of its members in accordance with law and till such time the Board ofthe respondent No. 1 may be declared to be without authority and hence void; It is further prayed that F&P Regulations in so far as they transgress into the exclusive statutory domain of the Respondent No.1 may be declared as ultra vires the PTRA 1996 and hence void; Ad-interim relief in terms of restraining the Respondents from allowing commencement of services under the subject 850MHz spectrum block be also granted"

W.P.No.2983-2016
list#10.74

text#20.88
The relevant facts are that the petitioners
text#30.85
acquired spectrum through auction/purchase from respondents No.1 & 2. They are aggrieved of subsequent allocation/sale of another spectrum to respondent No.4 on account of the fact that it caused disturbances, as a result whereof, filter had to be installed and cost was incurred. 3.
text#40.88
Learned counsel for the petitioners, inter
text#50.87
alia, contended that subsequent allocation of 850MHz Spectrum to respondent No.4 is without lawful authority inasmuch as it caused disturbances and the petitioners had to make remedial methods for smooth running of the operations. It was contended that petitioners since incurred cost for taking appropriate measures, hence respondents No.1 & 2 are obliged to compensate the petitioners. At this juncture, learned counsel for respondent No.1 objected to the maintainability of the petition due to the fact that order for compensation cannot be passed in a petition under Article 199 of the Constitution without recording of evidence. 5.
text#60.87
Learned counsel for the petitioners
text#70.85
submitted that petitioners have no alternate remedy
text#80.79
under
text#90.81
inasmuch
text#100.66
as
text#110.85
Pakistan
text#120.85
Telecommunication Re-Organization Act, 1996, and license granted to the petitioners, there is a bar for invoking jurisdiction of civil court. Learned counsel also read out the relevant provisions. 6.
text#130.88
Be that as it may, after hearing learned
text#140.88
counsels for the parties, it transpired that petitioners seek compensation for the cost incurred by them for taking remedial measures due to disturbances caused by allocation of 850MHz spectrum to respondent No.4.

Since the controversy cannot be resolved
text#30.88
without recording evidence hence it is just and proper for the petitioners to approach the court of plenary jurisdiction for redressal of their grievances. In view of above, instant petition is
list#40.87
8. disposed off with the observation that petitioners may avail appropriate remedy before the court of competent jurisdiction against the respondents. It is pertinent to observe that the court, seized of the matter, shall decide the same without being influenced by any observation made hereinabove.

1[THE SOCIETIES REGISTRATION ACT, 1860]
text#10.88
2,3,4&5Act No. XXI of 1860
text#20.88
[21st May, 1860]
text#30.88
An Act for the Registration of Literary, Scientific and Charitable Societies.
text#40.88
Preamble. WHEREAS it is expedient that provision should be made for improving the legal
text#50.88
condition of societies established for the promotion of literature, science, or the fine arts, or for the diffusion of useful knowledge, 6[the diffusion of political education] or for charitable purposes; It is enacted as follows:—
list#60.93
1. Societies formed by memorandum of association and registration.—Any seven or
text#70.88
more persons associated for any literary, scientific or charitable purpose, or for any such purpose as is described in section 20 of this Act, may, by subscribing their names to a memorandum of association and filing the same with the Registrar of Joint-stock Companies 7[* * *] from themselves into a society under this Act.
list#80.93
2. Memorandum of association.—The memorandum of association shall contain the
text#90.88
following things (that is to say):—
text#100.88
the name of the society :
text#110.88
the objects of the society :
text#120.88
the names, addresses, and occupations of the governors, council, directors, committee or other governing body to whom, by the rules of the society, the management of its affairs is entrusted.

1Short title given by the Short Title Act, 1897 (XIV of 1897). 2The Act (with exception of the first four sections) is based on the Literary and Scientific Institutions Act No. XVII & XVIII Vict., c 112, ss. 20 et seq. It has been declared to be in force in all the Provinces and the Capital of the Federation, except the Scheduled Districts, by s. 3 of the Laws Local Extent Act No. XV of 1874. It has been declared to be in force in Baluchistan by the British Baluchistan Laws Regulation No. II of 1913, s. 3. It has been declared, by notification under s. 3(a) of the Scheduled Districts Act No. XIV of 1874, to be in force in the following Scheduled Districts, namely:— The Districts of Hazara, Peshawar, Kohat, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Dera Ghazi Khan. [Portions of the Districts of Hazara, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Dera Ghazi Khan and the Districts of Peshawar and Kohat now form the N.W.F.P., see Gazette of India., 1901, Pt. I, p. 857, and ibid., 1902, Pt. I, p. 575]. It has been extended, by notification under s. 5 of the last-mentioned Act, to the Scheduled District of Sind-See Gazette of India, 1880, Pt. I, p. 672.
